title: Gram-positive and Gram-negative walls
caption: Drawn to scale. A Gram-positive wall is a thick mesh of peptidoglycan that traps crystal violet, so the cell stains purple. A Gram-negative wall has only a thin peptidoglycan layer under an outer membrane of lipopolysaccharide; it loses the stain and is counterstained pink.
alt: Two cross-sections of a bacterial cell surface, drawn to the same scale: Gram-positive with a thick peptidoglycan layer over the plasma membrane, and Gram-negative with lipopolysaccharide, an outer membrane, a thin peptidoglycan layer and the periplasm over the plasma membrane.
description: Gram-positive (Staphylococcus): a peptidoglycan wall about 30 nm thick (20–80 nm), then the plasma membrane. It keeps crystal violet and stains purple.
Gram-negative (E. coli): lipopolysaccharide on an outer membrane, a thin peptidoglycan layer (2–7 nm), the periplasm, then the plasma membrane. It loses crystal violet and is counterstained pink.
The outer membrane keeps many antibiotics away from the Gram-negative wall.
